title: PRD: Build a deterministic P&ID QA query layer
description:
## Problem Statement

Process engineers need a trustworthy way to ask questions about a DEXPI 1.3 source file without receiving non-deterministic or hallucinated answers from graph RAG or free-form LLM QA.

The current repository can extract a pyDEXPI full graph, persist a canonical base fact layer, derive an initial generic graph utility layer, and run a narrow pump discharge-path verifier. What it does not yet prove is whether Souffle can serve as the deterministic QA and verification engine over those generated facts.

The user wants to preserve the key product principle: LLMs may help classify, route, and explain questions later, but compliance answers must come from deterministic query outputs. Before adding any LLM integration, the backend must demonstrate that generated Datalog facts can answer useful P&ID topology questions, expose missing facts and predicates clearly, and preserve query results as auditable artifacts.

## Solution

Build the first deterministic P&ID QA query layer around generated derived graph semantics.

The solution should enrich the derived Datalog fact surface with enough base object facts to make query output interpretable, starting with node and node_label facts. It should add a small query corpus that records supported, unsupported, and future candidate P&ID QA questions in an engine-portable way. It should add a CLI query harness that runs a supported known-object topology query against an existing derived_graph_semantics.dl file using Souffle, prints readable terminal output, persists the combined Souffle program, persists a JSON result artifact, and keeps raw Souffle output files in an internal output directory.

The first supported query should compare reachable targets and downstream_reference targets for a known source object ID. The first near-term unsupported query should be a pump discharge path classification question. A harder manual-valve-before-check-valve question should be recorded as a future candidate so the system does not overfit only easy queries.

The query corpus should explicitly encode determinism requirements and LLM role constraints. LLM integration is out of scope for this PRD, but the corpus should make future LLM routing safe by documenting that LLMs may classify questions, route to deterministic queries, and explain deterministic results, but may not produce compliance answers without deterministic query output.

## User Stories

1. As a process engineer, I want to ask deterministic questions about a DEXPI 1.3 source file, so that I can trust the answer is repeatable and auditable.
2. As a process engineer, I want QA answers to come from deterministic query execution rather than free-form LLM generation, so that compliance answers do not vary between runs.
3. As a process engineer, I want to provide a known object ID and see what objects are reachable from it, so that I can inspect the topology around a specific P&ID object.
4. As a process engineer, I want to compare reachable targets with downstream_reference targets, so that I can understand whether the generic graph utility layer is too broad or too narrow.
5. As a process engineer, I want query output to show full object IDs and object labels, so that results are exact and still readable.
6. As a process engineer, I want empty query results to be treated as successful answers, so that no-result cases can teach us about isolated objects or missing semantics.
7. As a process engineer, I want a warning when the provided source ID is absent from node facts, so that I can distinguish an empty answer from a likely wrong ID.
8. As a process engineer, I want the system to clearly say when a question is unsupported, so that I do not receive a misleading answer.
9. As a process engineer, I want unsupported questions to explain whether facts or predicates are missing, so that I know what capability must be built next.
10. As a process engineer, I want future thermodynamic or hydraulic questions to be identified as requiring external calculation when appropriate, so that Datalog is not overclaimed as a physics engine.
11. As a process engineer, I want the near-term north-star query to trace and classify a centrifugal pump discharge path, so that the QA layer grows toward realistic P&ID review tasks.
12. As a process engineer, I want harder valve-ordering questions to remain visible as future candidates, so that the roadmap reflects realistic engineering concerns.
13. As a maintainer, I want graph_facts.json to remain the canonical base fact layer, so that extraction output stays stable and auditable.
14. As a maintainer, I want Souffle to be evaluated as the deterministic QA and verification engine, so that rule answers can be fast and repeatable.
15. As a maintainer, I want Python to orchestrate extraction, Datalog generation, Souffle execution, and artifact persistence, so that Python is not the source of truth for compliance answers.
16. As a maintainer, I want derived_graph_semantics.dl to include node and node_label facts, so that Datalog queries can produce readable P&ID information without falling back to graph_facts.json for every label.
17. As a maintainer, I want the query harness to operate on an existing derived_graph_semantics.dl file first, so that the first slice directly tests the artifact users want to query.
18. As a maintainer, I want the long-term design to allow querying from graph_facts.json directly, so that later workflows can generate and query Datalog in one command.
19. As a maintainer, I want missing Souffle installation to produce a clear diagnostic, so that setup problems are not confused with query failures.
20. As a maintainer, I want Souffle syntax or runtime failures to be treated as failed query execution, so that invalid query programs are surfaced clearly.
21. As a maintainer, I want unsupported corpus entries to return structured unsupported diagnostics, so that unsupported questions are first-class product outputs rather than errors.
22. As a maintainer, I want the query corpus to be separate from compliance rule YAML, so that QA questions do not get confused with promoted validation rules.
23. As a maintainer, I want one YAML file per query corpus entry, so that each query can have its own lifecycle, documentation, and promotion status.
24. As a maintainer, I want query corpus entries to include determinism metadata, so that the engine and source-of-truth assumptions are explicit.
25. As a maintainer, I want query corpus entries to include allowed and disallowed LLM roles, so that future LLM integration does not bypass deterministic execution.
26. As a maintainer, I want query corpus entries to include engine candidates such as Souffle and ErgoAI, so that the query library stays portable across deterministic engines.
27. As a maintainer, I want ErgoAI to remain a future engine candidate rather than an immediate dependency, so that the first slice tests the fact model before changing reasoning engines.
28. As a maintainer, I want the first query harness to read the query corpus entry minimally, so that the corpus becomes load-bearing without requiring a generic query interpreter too early.
29. As a maintainer, I want the first supported query implementation to be explicit and narrow, so that the team learns from real query output before inventing a broad abstraction.
30. As a maintainer, I want the combined Souffle program that actually ran to be persisted, so that users can inspect and rerun the exact query.
31. As a maintainer, I want the generated temporary query Datalog text included in the JSON result artifact, so that query behavior remains explainable.
32. As a maintainer, I want raw Souffle output files kept in an internal subdirectory, so that advanced users can inspect them while the top-level output remains readable.
33. As a maintainer, I want query output files to be overwritten during early experimentation, so that the learning loop stays low-friction.
34. As a maintainer, I want persisted JSON query artifacts, so that query behavior can become regression-tested and compared across fixtures.
35. As a maintainer, I want terminal output for the first query, so that hands-on learning stays tangible.
36. As a future LLM integrator, I want a query corpus with supported and unsupported entries, so that an LLM can later classify and route questions safely.
37. As a future LLM integrator, I want deterministic query outputs to be the only source of compliance answers, so that natural-language explanations remain grounded.
38. As a future rule author, I want the query corpus to reveal missing predicates, so that the P&ID query library grows from real questions instead of imagined ontology.
39. As a future rule author, I want the CodeQL-style library idea to grow from supported queries, so that raw graph facts become stable engineering predicates, reusable path predicates, and validation templates only when needed.
40. As a reviewer, I want the first query corpus to include a future candidate that is too hard today, so that the project does not optimize only for easy topology questions.
41. As a reviewer, I want the query corpus to classify unsupported questions by reason, so that missing data, missing predicates, external calculations, and ambiguity are not conflated.
42. As a reviewer, I want a clear distinction between unsupported_missing_facts and unsupported_missing_predicates, so that the roadmap can separate extraction work from query-library work.
43. As a reviewer, I want a clear distinction between unsupported_external_calculation and deterministic graph QA, so that thermodynamics and hydraulics are not accidentally oversold.
44. As a reviewer, I want a clear distinction between needs_human_clarification and deterministic query execution, so that ambiguous engineering questions are handled honestly.
45. As a reviewer, I want the first deterministic QA seam to be tested through the CLI and persisted artifacts, so that behavior is verified at the same level users experience it.

## Implementation Decisions

- The canonical base fact layer remains graph_facts.json.
- Souffle is the current deterministic engine for the first QA viability slice.
- Python remains the orchestration Adapter for generation, execution, diagnostics, terminal rendering, and artifact persistence.
- LLM integration is explicitly deferred until deterministic tools and query corpus semantics are established.
- The derived graph semantics output should be enriched with node and node_label facts.
- The first query harness operates on an existing derived_graph_semantics.dl file.
- The first supported query compares reachable and downstream_reference results for a known source object ID.
- The command should accept a query ID and load the corresponding query corpus entry.
- The command should support the first query ID with explicit implementation rather than a generic YAML-driven query interpreter.
- Unsupported query corpus entries should produce structured unsupported artifacts, not unknown-query errors.
- Missing Souffle should produce a clear diagnostic and failed status.
- Empty result sets should produce successful query artifacts.
- Source ID absence should produce a warning when node facts make validation possible, not a failed status.
- Terminal output should include full target IDs and labels.
- JSON output should include status, diagnostics, query metadata, source ID, generated query Datalog, combined program path, raw output directory, and result sets.
- The combined Souffle program should be persisted as a first-class artifact.
- Raw Souffle output files should be placed under an internal output subdirectory.
- Query output files may be overwritten during the viability phase.
- Query corpus entries should live under queries/corpus as separate YAML files.
- The first corpus entry should be compare_known_object_reachability with supported_deterministic status.
- The near-term target corpus entry should be classify_pump_discharge_path with unsupported_missing_predicates status.
- The advanced future candidate should be manual_valve_before_check_valve_with_exceptions with future_candidate status.
- Query corpus entries should include determinism metadata, current engine, future engine candidates, and LLM role constraints.
- ErgoAI should be documented as a future engine candidate for richer explanations, exceptions, and semantic-rule authoring, not adopted in the first slice.
- The long-term concept is a P&ID query library inspired by CodeQL: raw graph facts to stable engineering predicates to reusable path predicates to validation templates.
- The corpus should be engine-portable and should not make Souffle the only possible long-term reasoning engine.
- The near-term north-star query is pump discharge path classification rather than the more advanced manual-valve-before-check-valve query.

## Testing Decisions

- Good tests should verify behavior through public interfaces and persisted artifacts, not private helper structure.
- The highest test seam for the first slice is the CLI query command over a generated derived graph semantics file.
- Tests should run the query command against a representative fixture and assert terminal-visible behavior plus persisted JSON artifact shape.
- Tests should verify that derive-graph-semantics emits node and node_label facts as part of the generated Datalog artifact.
- Tests should verify that the first supported query returns successful output even when one or both result sets are empty.
- Tests should verify that absent source IDs produce warning diagnostics rather than failed execution.
- Tests should verify missing Souffle handling if feasible without depending on the developer machine PATH; if not feasible, isolate that behavior behind the command seam with controlled PATH configuration.
- Tests should verify unsupported corpus entries return structured unsupported diagnostics.
- Tests should verify the combined Souffle program is persisted and includes the generated query Datalog.
- Tests should verify raw Souffle output files are placed under an internal subdirectory.
- Tests should verify the checked-in query corpus entries include determinism and LLM-role metadata.
- Existing prior art includes CLI-style tests for export-facts, derive-graph-semantics, verify-suite, verify-raw-fixture, and compile-rule.
- Existing prior art also includes persisted artifact assertions for graph facts, derived graph semantics, verifier results, and behavioral harness summaries.
- The tests should extend those existing black-box seams rather than introducing internal mocks.
- The first implementation should use red-green vertical slices: one behavior test, minimal implementation, repeat.

## Out of Scope

- LLM integration.
- Natural-language question classification.
- RAG or MCP routing.
- OmniTQA implementation.
- ErgoAI integration.
- A generic query language interpreter over YAML corpus files.
- Full support for arbitrary user-generated P&ID questions.
- Full compliance rule authoring.
- Thermodynamic, hydraulic, sizing, or simulation calculations.
- DEXPI 2.0 ingestion.
- Replacing graph_facts.json as the canonical base fact layer.
- Making Python the source of truth for compliance answers.
- Immutable production run directories for query artifacts.
- A polished process engineer UI.
- Full path provenance or ordered path reconstruction beyond what the first query needs.
- Supporting the advanced manual-valve-before-check-valve query in the first slice.
- Promoting unsupported corpus entries to trusted validation rules.

## Further Notes

The key product principle is: the LLM can help ask, route, and explain the question, but deterministic tools must answer compliance questions.

The first implementation should be treated as a Souffle QA viability slice. It should be allowed to reveal that current predicates are too broad, too narrow, or missing. That learning is valuable and should drive the next predicates in the P&ID query library.

The strongest external architecture analogues are CodeQL for layered query libraries and query metadata, OPA for deterministic policy decisions and diagnostics, osquery for exposing messy domain state through stable queryable relations, and Semgrep or dbt-style registries for curated query/rule corpora with examples and tests.

The most important immediate learning is whether generated Datalog artifacts can support useful known-object topology QA before the project invests in YAML-to-rule compilation, LLM routing, or a larger semantic-rule engine.

title: Delete legacy query corpus, rule compiler, and XML-normalization paths
description:
## Problem

After reorganizing the package by pipeline seams, several compatibility paths still keep old architecture alive:

- queries/corpus/ YAML query entries and the query-derived-graph corpus loader.
- rules/ YAML inputs and compiled rule artifacts used by compile-rule tests.
- pydexpi_datalog/_legacy/ XML-direct normalization and cache paths used by dry-run/review-only compatibility behavior.
- Legacy JSON rule evaluation and patch proposal paths that depend on XML-direct normalized objects rather than graph-mirrored facts or LLM-native logic requests.

These paths assume humans hand-author structured YAML/query/rule files. In the LLM-native architecture, the user-facing authoring seam is a logic request: the LLM drafts Datalog plus an English restatement as an in-memory or persisted logic-request artifact, while deterministic execution remains the answer source.

## What to build

Delete the legacy query corpus, rule compiler artifacts, and XML-direct normalization paths. Keep or replace only the behavior that still belongs in the current architecture.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Delete queries/corpus/ and remove code/tests/docs that require YAML query-corpus entries.
- [ ] Delete rules/ and remove the compile-rule command, compiler tests, and compiled-rule fixture expectations unless a current non-legacy workflow still needs them.
- [ ] Delete pydexpi_datalog/_legacy/ and tests/_legacy/.
- [ ] Remove dry-run and review-only dependencies on legacy XML normalization/cache artifacts, or replace them with graph-facts/derived-semantics based behavior.
- [ ] Remove or rewrite legacy JSON rule evaluation and patch proposal tests that assume XML-direct normalized objects.
- [ ] Update README and docs so they describe the LLM-native logic-request path and no longer present YAML query/rule authoring as a supported workflow.
- [ ] Public CLI help no longer advertises removed commands.
- [ ] Full test suite passes after obsolete tests are removed or replaced.

## Notes

This is intentionally behavior-breaking cleanup. Do not treat it as a compatibility-preserving refactor. If a command or test only exists to preserve the old hand-authored YAML/query/rule workflow, remove it rather than moving it.

Keep the stable deterministic substrate:

- DEXPI source file to pyDEXPI full graph.
- graph_facts.json base fact artifact.
- graph_facts.dl and derived_graph_semantics.dl.
- BYOK logic requests that can draft Datalog and restatements against the approved predicate contract.

- pydexpi-datalog-1-3qo.8

title: Resolve source-rooted queries by deterministic object selectors
description:
## Parent

- pydexpi-datalog-1-153 PRD: Build a deterministic P&ID QA query layer

## What to build

Make source-rooted deterministic QA queries usable without requiring users to know internal graph node IDs. The query command should accept deterministic object selectors and resolve them through Datalog facts/predicates from the combined derived graph semantics artifact.

Allowed source selectors:

- --source-id for exact/debug/test use
- --source-tag for human-facing equipment tags such as P-4713
- --source-proteus-id for source Proteus IDs such as CentrifugalPump-1

Do not add --source-label. Class labels are too loose and commonly non-unique.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] query-derived-graph accepts --source-tag and --source-proteus-id for source-rooted supported queries.
- [ ] --source-id remains supported for exact tests and debugging.
- [ ] Source selector resolution uses Datalog output from the combined artifact, not Python parsing of graph_facts.json.
- [ ] Source-rooted supported queries fail clearly if no source selector is provided.
- [ ] If multiple selectors are provided and resolve to the same node, the query succeeds and records the resolved source ID.
- [ ] If multiple selectors resolve to different nodes, the query fails with a structured diagnostic.
- [ ] If a selector matches no node, the query fails with a structured diagnostic.
- [ ] If a selector matches multiple nodes, the query fails with an ambiguity diagnostic.
- [ ] Query corpus entries for compare_known_object_reachability and compare_direct_process_connections mark source selection as source-rooted.

## Notes

This bead should not add source-label selection and should not default source-rooted queries to the first graph node.
close_reason: Implemented deterministic source selectors for source-rooted queries. Validation: .venv/bin/python -m unittest discover -s tests (81 tests OK).

title: Add whole-P&ID query mode without first-node defaults
description:
## Parent

- pydexpi-datalog-1-153 PRD: Build a deterministic P&ID QA query layer

## What to build

Add query corpus and harness support for whole-P&ID deterministic queries that evaluate across the complete P&ID instead of treating an arbitrary graph node as a root.

Do not default source-rooted queries to the first node in the graph. NetworkX insertion order and container-like nodes such as ConceptualModel are not meaningful engineering defaults.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Query corpus metadata can distinguish source-rooted queries from whole_pid queries.
- [ ] Whole-P&ID queries run without requiring --source-id, --source-tag, or --source-proteus-id.
- [ ] Source-rooted queries still require an explicit source selector.
- [ ] The query harness rejects accidental first-node default behavior.
- [ ] A first whole-P&ID query entry exists in the corpus, focused on a realistic P&ID-wide question rather than generic reachability.
- [ ] Whole-P&ID query artifacts record that the scope was the whole P&ID, not a selected source node.
- [ ] Tests prove a whole-P&ID query can run or return a structured unsupported/future-candidate artifact without a source selector.

## Notes

This is likely the precursor to all-pump discharge-path classification. Keep it separate from source selector work so source-rooted and whole-P&ID query semantics remain explicit.
close_reason: Implemented whole-P&ID query scope metadata and future-candidate query artifacts without source selector defaults. Validation: .venv/bin/python -m unittest discover -s tests (84 tests OK).

title: Emit human-readable node alias facts in derived graph semantics
description:
Add a thin alias layer to derived graph semantics so deterministic QA can keep node_id as the canonical topology key while exposing human-readable selectors for tests and terminal output.

Context:
- Parent PRD: pydexpi-datalog-1-153 Build a deterministic P&ID QA query layer.
- Current derived semantics emits node/1 and node_label/2 from graph_facts.json.
- UUID node IDs are correct for graph joins but hard for humans to inspect against P&ID/SVG/XML views.

What to build:
- Keep node_id as the canonical graph identity.
- Emit node_tag(id, tag) facts from node attribute tagName when present.
- Emit node_proteus_id(id, proteus_id) facts from node attribute proteusId when present.
- Consider emitting node_display_name(id, display) with a narrow deterministic fallback order: tagName, then proteusId, then label.
- Do not replace node_id in existing predicates.
- Do not parse SVG labels or introduce a generic identity resolver in this slice.

Acceptance criteria:
- derive-graph-semantics emits node_tag/2 for tagged graph objects.
- derive-graph-semantics emits node_proteus_id/2 for objects with proteusId.
- If node_display_name/2 is included, its fallback order is documented and tested.
- Existing node/1, node_label/2, and edge-family predicates continue to be emitted unchanged.
- Tests verify behavior through the CLI-generated derived_graph_semantics.dl artifact using representative graph_facts.json.
- Representative generated artifact is updated if this repo keeps one checked in.
close_reason: Completed: derive-graph-semantics now emits node_tag/2 from tagName and node_proteus_id/2 from proteusId while keeping node_id as the canonical graph identity. Updated representative derived_graph_semantics.dl, CLI artifact tests, and the derived graph semantics contract. Validation passed: .venv/bin/python -m unittest discover -s tests -p test_derive_graph_semantics.py (4 tests OK) and .venv/bin/python -m unittest discover -s tests (58 tests OK).

title: Define stable reported result schemas for graph-based rule evaluation
description:
## Parent

- PRD: GitHub issue #1 "Build graph-to-facts Datalog verifier on top of a pyDEXPI fork"

## What to build

Define the stable reported result schemas for graph-based rule evaluation over the first discharge-path rule family.

Given graph-mirrored facts and compiled Datalog rules, lock the machine-readable output shapes for `pass`, `hard_violation`, `bounded_failure_off_page`, and `evaluation_diagnostic`. Each result shape must carry deterministic evidence about the traversed path, matched objects, matched edges, boundary kind, and short human-readable explanation.

This slice should make the reporting model concrete before the fixture suite is expanded.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Stable machine-readable result schemas exist for `pass`, `hard_violation`, `bounded_failure_off_page`, and `evaluation_diagnostic`.
- [ ] Example output artifacts exist for each result shape and show the required path and boundary evidence.
- [ ] The required evidence for each result shape is documented, including matched objects, traversed edges, terminal boundary, and human-readable message.
- [ ] The result shapes are deterministic enough to be reused as golden outputs in later fixture-driven tests.

title: Establish the graph-to-facts contract from pinned pyDEXPI outputs
description:
## Parent

- PRD: GitHub issue #1 "Build graph-to-facts Datalog verifier on top of a pyDEXPI fork"

## What to build

Establish the project-owned graph-to-facts contract over pinned `pyDEXPI` output for several real DEXPI 1.3 pump-related examples already in the repo.

title: PRD: OSS web UI single-file review workflow
description:
## Problem Statement

OSS users currently have to interact with DEXPI-datalog through CLI and persisted artifacts. That makes the deterministic P&ID QA workflow inspectable, but it is not approachable for a process engineer who wants to upload one DEXPI 1.3 source file, inspect the resulting topology, ask a question, review the generated logic, and receive a grounded answer with evidence.

The next major product move is a web UI that preserves the repository's deterministic trust boundary while making the single-file review session usable: DEXPI XML upload, asynchronous preparation, process-topology visualization, provider-neutral BYOK settings, logic-request refinement, confirmation, deterministic execution, evidence highlighting, and selected rule-pack query execution.

## Solution

Build an OSS web UI with a real Python backend API and a separate React/TypeScript frontend using TSX components. The backend remains in the same Python package/process as the existing deterministic pipeline and calls library functions directly rather than shelling out to the CLI. The frontend uses a graph visualization library, preferably Cytoscape.js, to show a process-topology view after upload.

The user-facing logic-request review workflow is scoped to one active single-file review session in the first vertical slice, with explicit session IDs in the backend API. A user uploads one DEXPI 1.3 source file, receives asynchronous session preparation status, and then sees readiness metadata plus a compact topology-view model. The query/refinement UI remains disabled until extraction and derived graph semantics are ready.

The assistant panel supports free-form logic requests with optional examples. A selected topology object can prefill the visible source scope, but that scope must be explicit and editable before refinement or drafting. The Improve action routes the request first; topology QA logic requests receive a reviewable refinement, while documentation, metadata, clarification, raw-attribute, and missing-capability paths are handled without forcing everything into Datalog.

After refinement is accepted, the workflow drafts generated Datalog and a Datalog-grounded plain-English restatement. The primary confirmation object is the plain-English restatement; Datalog is inspectable but not directly editable in OSS v1. Once confirmed, deterministic execution produces a concise grounded logic-request answer with expandable evidence and evidence highlighting in the topology view.

Standard checks are separate selected rule-pack queries. They do not run automatically after upload, and they do not require LLM-style confirmation because they are already validated rule-pack logic. Results use the same answer/evidence posture and topology evidence highlighting where possible.

Provider-neutral BYOK is supported from the start. OSS v1 uses a global session-level provider/model setting, exposes provider/model/configured status to the UI, never exposes secret values, and records provider/model metadata per logic-request audit record. Credentials may be entered through local application settings and retained only in the local provider credential store; they must not be persisted to project artifacts or logs.

Artifacts are temporary by default in OSS v1. Uploaded XML, generated artifacts, logic requests, rule-pack results, and topology data live for the active review session unless the user explicitly exports or downloads them. Future signed-in persistence should organize history as review projects containing single-file review sessions, not as a flat chat history.

## User Stories

1. As an OSS user, I want to upload one DEXPI 1.3 source file, so that I can begin a single-file review session without using the CLI.
2. As an OSS user, I want the upload screen to reject non-DEXPI XML inputs with a normalized diagnostic, so that I understand why the file cannot be reviewed.
3. As an OSS user, I want raw parser details to be expandable after an upload failure, so that I can troubleshoot pyDEXPI-specific failures when needed.
4. As an OSS user, I want session preparation to run as an asynchronous job, so that the UI can show progress rather than freezing during extraction and derivation.
5. As an OSS user, I want to retry a failed upload or session preparation job, so that transient or corrected input problems do not require restarting the app.
6. As an OSS user, I want the query controls disabled until graph facts and derived graph semantics are ready, so that I do not ask questions against an unprepared substrate.
7. As an OSS user, I want readiness metadata after upload, so that I can see whether the session is ready, failed, or still running.
8. As an OSS user, I want a compact topology-view model returned after preparation, so that the web UI can render the review view without parsing internal artifacts directly.
9. As an OSS user, I want the center of the loaded app to show a topology review view, so that the uploaded engineering graph is the primary object of work.
10. As an OSS user, I want the topology review view to show curated process-topology relationships by default, so that I see meaningful equipment and connection structure instead of a raw graph dump.
11. As an OSS user, I want advanced raw graph facts to be deferred behind a later layer toggle, so that the v1 view remains understandable.
12. As an OSS user, I want stable artifact IDs in the topology view model, so that visual selections and deterministic evidence refer to the same objects.
13. As an OSS user, I want to select an object in the topology view, so that it can become the source scope for a logic request.
14. As an OSS user, I want selected source scope shown explicitly in the assistant panel, so that hidden visual context does not change the generated query unexpectedly.
15. As an OSS user, I want to remove or change the visible source scope, so that I can ask whole-file or different-object questions deliberately.
16. As an OSS user, I want a right-side assistant panel after upload, so that I can ask logic requests while keeping the topology view visible.
17. As an OSS user, I want a free-form prompt composer, so that I can write natural questions in my own words.
18. As an OSS user, I want optional example prompt chips, so that I can discover useful query shapes without being forced into a form.
19. As an OSS user, I want an Improve action, so that vague questions can be sharpened before logic is generated.
20. As an OSS user, I want Improve to produce a reviewable refinement, so that the app never silently rewrites my intent.
21. As an OSS user, I want the refinement to include assumptions and recommended scope where relevant, so that I can catch misunderstandings early.
22. As an OSS user, I want routing to happen before model-backed refinement, so that documentation, metadata, clarification, and unsupported requests are handled faithfully.
23. As an OSS user, I want unsupported requests to stop with a missing-capability explanation, so that the app does not invent answers.
24. As an OSS user, I want unsupported-request details to be copyable or downloadable, so that they can inform future predicate or rule-pack work.
25. As an OSS user, I want accepted refinements to lead to generated Datalog plus a plain-English restatement, so that I can review the intended deterministic query.
26. As an OSS user, I want primary confirmation to focus on the plain-English restatement, so that I can approve query semantics without reading Datalog syntax.
27. As an OSS user, I want generated Datalog to remain visible or expandable, so that power users can inspect the executable counterpart.
28. As an OSS user, I do not want to edit generated Datalog directly in v1, so that query changes continue through the reviewable natural-language workflow.
29. As an OSS user, I want each logic request to be independent, so that hidden chat history does not affect query semantics.
30. As an OSS user, I want confirmed logic requests reusable within the active temporary session, so that I can repeat useful queries without creating a persistent rule library.
31. As an OSS user, I want the confirmed query to execute as a job, so that long-running deterministic work has consistent status and result handling.
32. As an OSS user, I want a concise deterministic answer first, so that I can quickly understand the result.
33. As an OSS user, I want expandable deterministic evidence behind every answer, so that I can audit matched nodes, edges, paths, result rows, and generated query context.
34. As an OSS user, I want evidence highlighting in the topology review view, so that the answer is visually tied to source scope, matched objects, and evidence paths.
35. As an OSS user, I want rule-pack queries presented separately from user-authored logic requests, so that I understand which checks are standard product logic and which are ad hoc generated logic.
36. As an OSS user, I want rule-pack queries to run only when explicitly selected, so that upload does not trigger surprise analysis.
37. As an OSS user, I want selected rule-pack queries to execute directly, so that validated standard checks do not require unnecessary confirmation.
38. As an OSS user, I want rule-pack results to show concise outcomes with expandable evidence, so that standard checks are as auditable as logic-request answers.
39. As an OSS user, I want all review workflow jobs to expose coarse status, so that I can distinguish queued, running, succeeded, and failed work.
40. As an OSS user, I want jobs to include optional stage text, so that I can see whether the system is extracting graph facts, deriving semantics, refining, drafting, executing, or running a rule pack.
41. As an OSS user, I want one active session in the first vertical slice, so that the app stays simple and focused.
42. As a future product user, I want backend session IDs from v1, so that async jobs, artifacts, retry, and later persistence have stable references.
43. As an OSS user, I want provider-neutral BYOK settings, so that the app is not conceptually limited to one model provider.
44. As an OSS user, I want OpenAI to be supportable first without hard-coding the settings model to OpenAI only, so that other providers can be added later.
45. As an OSS user, I want provider and model selection to be global for the active session, so that I do not have to configure every logic request separately.
46. As an OSS user, I want provider/model metadata recorded per request, so that exported audit artifacts remain reproducible.
47. As an OSS user, I want to see provider name, selected model, and configured/not configured status, so that I know whether model-backed steps can run.
48. As an OSS user, I never want the frontend or API responses to reveal secret key values, so that provider credentials remain private.
49. As an OSS user, I want to enter provider credentials through local application settings, so that the web UI works as an app rather than requiring only shell environment setup.
50. As an OSS user, I want local application settings to make clear that credentials stay local, so that I understand the BYOK boundary.
51. As an OSS user, I want provider credentials excluded from project artifacts, audit bundles, and logs, so that exported review material does not leak secrets.
52. As an OSS user, I want uploaded XML and generated artifacts to be temporary by default, so that engineering files are not silently retained.
53. As an OSS user, I want explicit export or download for artifacts I choose to keep, so that persistence is intentional.
54. As a future signed-in user, I want persistent history organized as review projects containing single-file review sessions, so that engineering context is not reduced to flat chat history.
55. As a future signed-in user, I want rendered images or topology snapshots treated as convenience views, so that uploaded XML and deterministic artifacts remain the source of truth.
56. As a developer, I want the web backend to call library functions directly, so that the API does not shell out to the CLI for core workflow orchestration.
57. As a developer, I want coarse workflow endpoints for product actions, so that the frontend does not orchestrate internal pipeline steps directly.
58. As a developer, I want lower-level library seams preserved, so that CLI and tests continue to use inspectable deterministic artifacts.
59. As a developer, I want the frontend built inside this repo for v1, so that the OSS version evolves as one product.
60. As a developer, I want a React frontend or equivalent mainstream framework, so that the nontrivial UI state machine is explicit and maintainable.
61. As a developer, I want a graph visualization library, so that pan, zoom, selection, layout, and highlighting are not rebuilt from scratch.
62. As a developer, I want Cytoscape.js considered the default visualization library, so that the process-topology view is optimized for inspectable graph interaction rather than node-editor behavior.
63. As a developer, I want frontend components written in TypeScript/TSX, so that UI state, API contracts, and graph view models are typed as the web UI grows.

## Implementation Decisions

- The v1 product is a user-facing logic-request review workflow scoped to an OSS single-file review session.
- The term "harness" should not be used for the product flow because this repo already uses harness-like language for verifier behavior tests.
- The upload input accepts DEXPI 1.3 XML only.
- The topology center pane is a topology review view, not a layout-faithful generated P&ID or source drawing replica.
- The default visual surface is the process-topology view: curated process/topology relationships, not every extracted graph fact.
- The topology-view model should use stable canonical base fact layer object IDs and derive process/topology edges from the derived semantics/predicate layer where possible.
- Query and refinement controls remain disabled until session preparation has completed successfully.
- Session preparation is asynchronous and returns readiness metadata plus a compact topology-view model.
- Review workflow work is consistently job-shaped: session preparation, refinement, drafting, deterministic query execution, and rule-pack execution all expose job status and result artifacts.
- Jobs expose stable coarse status and optional human-readable stage text.
- Upload retry is required; cancellation is optional for v1.
- The first UI exposes one active session, but the backend API uses explicit session IDs from v1.
- The backend API should expose coarse workflow endpoints aligned with product actions such as upload/session preparation, provider settings, refinement, drafting, confirmation, query execution, rule-pack execution, job status, and artifact download.
- The backend should live in the same Python package/process as the deterministic pipeline and call library functions directly.
- The CLI remains an inspectable artifact/debug surface, not the web backend's orchestration mechanism.
- The frontend is a separate JS application calling the Python API.
- The frontend should use React or another mainstream component framework.
- The frontend should be written in TypeScript with TSX components rather than plain JavaScript/JSX.
- The topology visualization should use a graph visualization library; Cytoscape.js is the recommended default unless a prototype proves another library better.
- The loaded UI prioritizes the topology review view, with the prompt composer and review workflow in the right-side assistant panel.
- Before upload, the app may use a calm centered upload/composer layout inspired by Harvey-style interaction, but without implying a vault or multi-document project in OSS v1.
- Selecting an object in the topology view can prefill visible source scope, but scope must be shown explicitly and be editable/removable before refinement or drafting.
- Improve routes the request first and only performs model-backed refinement for topology QA logic requests.
- Logic-request refinement is reviewable and optional; it must not silently rewrite user intent.
- After accepted refinement, the app drafts generated Datalog and a Datalog-grounded plain-English restatement.
- Primary confirmation is the plain-English restatement, with Datalog available for inspection.
- Datalog is not directly editable in OSS v1.
- Confirmed logic requests may be reused within the active temporary session only.
- Each new logic request is independent and does not inherit hidden assumptions, hidden source scope, or prior answer context.
- Deterministic execution is the source of truth for answers.
- Final answer text is deterministically rendered in v1; an LLM explanation may be added later only behind the same evidence boundary.
- Answers show concise summaries first with expandable evidence.
- Evidence highlighting is part of v1 and should connect answers and rule-pack results back to source scope, matched objects, and evidence paths in the topology review view.
- Standard checks are selected rule-pack queries, not background upload-time analysis.
- Rule-pack queries execute directly once selected and do not use the LLM confirmation step.
- Provider-neutral BYOK settings are part of v1.
- The first supported provider adapter may be OpenAI, but settings and API concepts should be provider-neutral.
- Provider/model selection is global for the active OSS session and recorded per request in audit artifacts.
- The UI may display provider name, selected model, and configured/not configured status, but never secret values.
- Users may enter provider credentials through local application settings in OSS v1.
- Provider credentials are retained only in the local provider credential store and must not appear in project artifacts, audit bundles, logs, or API responses.
- Uploaded XML and generated artifacts are temporary session artifacts by default.
- Users may explicitly export/download session artifacts and diagnostics.
- Future signed-in persistence should organize saved history as review projects containing single-file review sessions.
- Future persisted images/topology snapshots are convenience views; uploaded XML and deterministic artifacts remain source of truth.
- User-uploaded policy/source documents for rule-pack synthesis are out of scope for this milestone.
- PDF, image, SVG, and multimodal source extraction are out of scope for this milestone.
- A short ADR should be created for the web architecture decision once implementation begins, covering the real backend API, same-process Python backend, separate React frontend, async job-shaped workflow, explicit session IDs, and graph-library topology view.

## Testing Decisions

- Tests should target public behavior and artifact/API contracts, not private implementation details.
- Existing public library tests are prior art for deriving graph semantics and evaluating rules from graph facts.
- Existing CLI/artifact tests are prior art for validating stable persisted output without testing private helpers.
- Existing LLM model-access tests are prior art for BYOK metadata, missing credential diagnostics, routing, source selection, generated Datalog, and formal restatement artifacts.
- Existing verifier tests are prior art for deterministic rule-pack result artifacts and behavior harness summaries.
- Add backend workflow/API tests at the highest seam possible: upload/session preparation returns job state and eventually readiness metadata plus topology-view model.
- Add API tests proving query/refinement endpoints reject or defer work until the session is ready.
- Add API tests for normalized upload diagnostics with raw parser details available behind a details field.
- Add API tests for retry behavior on failed preparation jobs.
- Add API tests for provider settings that expose provider/model/configured status without exposing secret values.
- Add tests proving credentials are not written to exported artifacts, logic-request audit artifacts, job results, or logs controlled by the application.
- Add routing/refinement tests proving Improve routes first and does not refine documentation, metadata, unsupported, or clarification requests into Datalog.
- Add tests proving accepted refinement leads to a draft artifact containing both generated Datalog and a Datalog-grounded restatement.
- Add confirmation tests proving the plain-English restatement is the primary confirmation object and that generated Datalog remains inspectable.
- Add tests proving direct Datalog edits are not accepted by the v1 workflow.
- Add execution tests proving confirmed queries run as jobs and produce grounded logic-request answers backed by deterministic result artifacts.
- Add tests proving final answer summaries are deterministically rendered from execution output for v1.
- Add evidence tests proving answer/result artifacts can drive source, matched-object, and path highlighting in the topology-view model.
- Add rule-pack API tests proving selected standard rule-pack queries execute directly and only when explicitly requested.
- Add frontend component/integration tests for disabled query state before readiness, visible source scope after topology selection, reviewable refinement, confirmation, job polling states, and evidence highlighting.
- Add frontend tests that provider settings never display raw credential values.
- Add frontend type-checking as part of validation so API response shapes, topology-view models, and TSX component props stay coherent.
- Avoid brittle visual pixel tests for graph layout; test semantic view-model mapping, selected IDs, evidence-highlight states, and user interaction outcomes.

## Out of Scope

- Multi-P&ID or multi-file OSS review sessions.
- A vault, project corpus, or persistent account history in OSS v1.
- Signed-in authentication and account-scoped persistence.
- Server-managed customer credential vaults.
- App-managed credit tier.
- Automatic standard check execution after upload.
- Direct Datalog editing.
- Implicit follow-up chat context.
- User-uploaded policy/source documents for rule-pack synthesis.
- PDF/image/SVG source extraction or multimodal diagram interpretation.
- Layout-faithful reconstruction of the source P&ID drawing.
- Cross-session saved rule libraries.
- Cancellation as a required v1 capability.
- Detailed progress percentages for jobs.
- Multiple visible active sessions in the first UI vertical slice.

## Further Notes

- The PRD intentionally preserves the existing product rule: deterministic execution output is the source of truth for P&ID QA and compliance answers. Natural-language systems may draft, refine, restate, route, and eventually explain, but they do not produce unsupported answers.
- The current repo already exposes useful lower-level seams: graph-fact export, derived graph semantics, rule evaluation, logic-request routing/drafting, source selection, and artifact validation. The web API should wrap those seams rather than replace them.
- The visual inspiration is a clean Harvey-style assistant experience and a P&ID-centered workspace, but the product language should avoid promising a vault or a generated source drawing in OSS v1.
- The glossary has been updated with the core product terms resolved during planning: user-facing logic-request review workflow, single-file review session, session preparation job, review workflow job, review project, temporary session artifact, session-scoped logic reuse, independent logic request, topology review view, process-topology view, evidence highlighting, visible source scope, logic-request confirmation, grounded logic-request answer, model provider credential, and local provider credential store.

title: Define full-page P&ID acceptance corpus and success matrix
description:
## Parent

pydexpi-datalog-1-37x

## What to build

Select or create the full-page DEXPI 1.3 P&ID acceptance documents that define OSS v1 success for the user-facing logic-request review workflow. These documents are the acceptance corpus for deterministic extraction, topology modeling, rule/query evidence, UI readiness, and diagnostics.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] At least 5 full-page DEXPI 1.3 P&ID acceptance documents are selected or created.
- [ ] The corpus includes simple pump/valve/line, pump/heat-exchanger, branching or merging topology, instrumentation-heavy topology, and intentionally problematic or incomplete topology.
- [ ] Documents are classified as public, sanitized, or synthetic; tiny XML fragments are rejected except for narrow parser-error tests.
- [ ] Each document records expected preparation, topology, query, rule-pack, evidence, and diagnostic outcomes.

title: PRD: Datalog confirmation and topology review UI
description:
## Problem Statement

The current assistant-ui frontend proves that a user can upload a DEXPI 1.3 source file, prepare a backend review session, render backend-derived topology nodes, and receive a deterministic backend answer. However, the product still hides the actual logic-request review workflow. Datalog reasoning prompts are collapsed into a one-line answer, graph selection can still feel like hidden query scope, non-Datalog prompts can fall back to generic placeholder text, and the graph panel remains a raw topology view rather than a process-engineer-facing inspection surface.

Process engineers need to ask bounded engineering questions in natural language, understand when the system is proposing generated Datalog, review that proposal before execution, and receive grounded answers with visible evidence. They also need a graph view that supports inspection and evidence highlighting without silently changing query scope.

## Solution

Build an OSS v1 user-facing logic-request review workflow where sending a prompt routes to the appropriate answer path. Graph lookup and bounded engineering answers can answer directly when faithful. Datalog reasoning prompts produce a structured confirmation card in the chat thread instead of auto-executing. The card presents plain-language meaning and reviewable query context first, keeps generated Datalog collapsed but inspectable, and requires explicit user approval before the Python backend runs the query.

The LLM may draft Datalog directly for the near-term prototype, using rich predicate and EDB/IDB context. The Python backend owns Datalog execution safety validation, not semantic proof. The user owns semantic approval through the confirmation card. The backend executes only after confirmation and returns a grounded logic-request answer with an always-visible evidence summary plus expandable raw details.

Graph interaction becomes inspection-only for OSS v1. Clicking graph nodes shows details and evidence roles but does not scope queries. Query scope comes from object tags or identifiers mentioned in prompt text and is shown for review in the confirmation card when relevant. The graph panel starts hidden, opens automatically after successful upload, can be manually closed or reopened, and auto-opens when deterministic evidence is available.

A later graph modernization slice should replace the hand-written SVG with a GraphML-backed topology graph, likely rendered with Cytoscape.js. The graph should use process-engineer-facing labels and typed shapes for equipment, instruments, lines, nozzles, piping nodes, network segments, and raw structural DEXPI objects. This is an interactive topology graph, not a layout-faithful P&ID drawing replica.

## User Stories

1. As a process engineer, I want to upload one DEXPI 1.3 XML file, so that I can start a single-file review session from source engineering data.
2. As a process engineer, I want the graph panel to start hidden, so that the first screen focuses on asking a question rather than a dense graph.
3. As a process engineer, I want the graph panel to open after upload, so that I can inspect prepared topology when it becomes available.
4. As a process engineer, I want to manually close and reopen the graph panel after upload, so that I control how much screen space it uses.
5. As a process engineer, I want graph selection to show inspection details only, so that clicking a node does not secretly change query semantics.
6. As a process engineer, I want graph details to tell me selection is for inspection only, so that I know to mention object tags in questions.
7. As a process engineer, I want to ask about a specific object by tag in the prompt, so that query scope is explicit in text.
8. As a process engineer, I want inferred object references to appear in the confirmation card, so that I can catch scope mistakes before execution.
9. As a process engineer, I want graph lookup questions to answer directly, so that simple facts like type, attributes, and direct connections do not require Datalog confirmation.
10. As a process engineer, I want Datalog reasoning questions to produce a confirmation card, so that generated logic never runs silently.
11. As a process engineer, I want confirmation cards inside the chat thread, so that approval happens in the same conversational flow as my question.
12. As a process engineer, I want the card to show plain-language meaning first, so that I can approve intended semantics without reading code first.
13. As a process engineer, I want generated Datalog available in an expandable section, so that I can inspect executable logic when needed.
14. As a process engineer, I want generated Datalog collapsed by default, so that raw logic does not dominate the normal review flow.
15. As a process engineer, I want validation status visible on the confirmation card, so that I know whether the query is safe to run.
16. As a process engineer, I want Run, Revise, and Cancel actions on the card, so that I can approve, repair, or reject generated logic.
17. As a process engineer, I want deterministic execution only after clicking Run, so that I control when generated logic is executed.
18. As a process engineer, I want a short evidence summary always visible in the answer, so that the answer is not just a one-line claim.
19. As a process engineer, I want raw evidence details expandable, so that I can inspect bindings, rows, paths, and provenance without cluttering the default answer.
20. As a process engineer, I want the graph panel to auto-open when an answer has evidence highlights, so that visual evidence is not hidden.
21. As a process engineer, I want highlighted nodes and paths in the graph, so that deterministic evidence is visually tied to topology.
22. As a process engineer, I want non-Datalog answers to be bounded engineering answers, so that the app does not become an open general chatbot.
23. As a process engineer, I want bounded engineering answers to say whether they used loaded P&ID facts, reference material, or general engineering knowledge, so that I understand the answer source posture.
24. As a process engineer, I want casual out-of-scope prompts to be redirected politely, so that the app remains focused on P&ID QA.
25. As a process engineer, I want compliance questions to require a loaded standard pack, so that the system does not answer compliance from model memory.
26. As a process engineer, I want unloaded standards to produce a missing-capability response, so that I know what data is required before a compliance check can run.
27. As a demo user, I want a tiny non-authoritative demo standard pack, so that I can see standards-backed Datalog confirmation and execution without relying on real legal content.
28. As a demo user, I want a simple pump discharge check, so that the demo proves graph reasoning without inventing an EPA claim.
29. As a developer, I want the LLM to draft Datalog with rich predicate context, so that the prototype can support useful questions without a large Python intent compiler.
30. As a developer, I want Python to validate Datalog execution safety, so that generated logic stays within session facts, approved predicates, output shape, filesystem boundary, and execution limits.
31. As a developer, I want validation to avoid proving semantic correctness, so that the implementation remains tractable and leaves meaning approval to the user.
32. As a developer, I want deterministic guardrails for obvious cases, so that no-session, out-of-scope, direct lookup, obvious Datalog, documentation, and unsupported requests are handled predictably.
33. As a developer, I want route decisions to stay quiet unless they require confirmation, clarification, or diagnostics, so that normal answers do not expose debug routing labels.
34. As a developer, I want graph lookup to be a backend capability, so that direct facts can be shared by chat answers, graph details, and search without model-owned graph querying.
35. As a developer, I want the confirmation workflow implemented before graph modernization, so that product correctness is solved before the graph renderer rewrite.
36. As a developer, I want graph modernization to use a GraphML-backed topology graph where possible, so that we can explore DEXPI2graphML-like conversion and better graph tooling.
37. As a process engineer, I want node labels to prioritize engineering tags, line numbers, instrument loop tags, and equipment names, so that the graph mirrors what I expect to see on a P&ID.
38. As a process engineer, I want unknown or raw nodes to use type plus short stable ID fallback labels, so that they remain inspectable without pretending to be engineering tags.
39. As a process engineer, I want node shapes to encode object classes, so that pumps, valves, instruments, nozzles, piping nodes, segments, and unknown objects are visually distinct.
40. As a process engineer, I want default unknown objects to render as circles, so that unsupported types still appear consistently.
41. As a process engineer, I want nozzles, piping nodes, network segments, and conceptual model objects to be visually de-emphasized or differently shaped, so that structural DEXPI objects do not dominate equipment reasoning.
42. As a process engineer, I want raw topology mode later, so that debugging can expose every DEXPI object when needed.

## Implementation Decisions

- Use the existing Python backend API as the server boundary. The browser and model provider do not execute Datalog.
- Preserve the repository-owned deterministic workflow seams from the accepted web review shell ADR.
- Use the existing domain language: hybrid QA request routing, topology QA logic request, logic-request confirmation, grounded logic-request answer, visual topology selection, text-derived query scope, and bounded engineering answer.
- Non-Datalog answers must be bounded engineering answers, not open general chat.
- Graph lookup requests are direct local fact requests for type, attributes, selected objects, or immediate connections.
- Datalog reasoning requests include derived relationships, recursion, standards, absence, constraints, multi-hop paths, and compliance logic.
- Graph lookup should be a deterministic backend capability, not primarily an LLM tool.
- Generated or newly drafted Datalog requires explicit Datalog execution approval before execution.
- The first confirmation implementation should use Send-to-confirmation flow rather than a separate Improve button.
- A Harvey-style Improve action is future refinement work, not required for the first confirmation-card slice.
- The LLM may draft Datalog directly in the near-term prototype when supplied with predicate contract and EDB/IDB context.
- Python validates execution safety and result contract, not semantic correctness.
- Minimum validation includes: append-only query behavior against prepared EDB/IDB, no arbitrary filesystem directives, approved predicates, allowed output shape, read-only execution, syntax check, query size limit, timeout, and row limit.
- Confirmation card is rendered inside the chat thread, not in the graph panel.
- Confirmation card prioritizes plain-language meaning and intent/context over raw Datalog.
- Generated Datalog is collapsed by default but available for inspection.
- Route labels should be quiet in normal answers and exposed only through user-action states or diagnostics.
- Evidence presentation should always include a short summary and expandable raw details.
- The graph panel starts hidden, auto-opens after successful upload, then is manually closeable/openable.
- The graph panel auto-opens when deterministic answer evidence is available.
- Graph selection is inspection-only in OSS v1 and must not implicitly scope chat queries.
- Text-derived query scope comes from tags or identifiers mentioned in the prompt and should be shown for review.
- Compliance and standards reasoning require a loaded standard pack.
- If a referenced standard pack is not loaded, return an unloaded-standard missing-capability response by default.
- A bounded explanation of an unloaded standard may be given only when explicitly requested.
- Include a tiny non-authoritative demo standard pack for OSS v1 demonstration.
- The first demo standard check should be a simple demo pump discharge check rather than a synthetic legal EPA claim.
- Split implementation into at least two major slices: confirmation workflow first, GraphML/Cytoscape graph modernization later.
- Graph modernization should target an interactive topology graph, not a layout-faithful P&ID drawing recreation.
- DEXPI2graphML should be treated as inspiration or a candidate conversion layer for GraphML-backed topology, not as a guaranteed faithful P&ID renderer.
- Node labels should prioritize engineering-facing labels: tag name, line number, instrument loop tag, equipment name, then type plus short stable ID fallback.
- Node styles should map object class to predefined shapes. Unknown/default objects use circles.

## Testing Decisions

- Test public product behavior, not private helper implementation.
- Prefer browser-level smoke tests for upload, graph visibility, confirmation card, Run action, answer evidence summary, expandable details, and graph evidence highlighting.
- Existing backend API tests are prior art for prepare, provider settings, improve, confirm, execute, rule-pack results, exports, and zero-secret-leak behavior.
- Existing Chainlit review flow tests are prior art for route-first Improve, non-topology routing, confirmation artifacts, generated Datalog, restatement-first confirmation, direct-edit prohibition, and evidence highlights.
- Existing LLM model-access tests are prior art for route behavior, missing credentials, provider-neutral BYOK, unsupported requests, and generated Datalog/restatement artifacts.
- Add route behavior tests for no-session, out-of-scope, direct graph lookup, obvious Datalog reasoning, documentation/predicate help, unsupported simulation/editing requests, and ambiguous bounded-engineering prompts.
- Add backend validation tests proving unsafe generated Datalog is rejected before confirmation or execution.
- Add confirmation-card frontend tests proving generated Datalog is collapsed by default and Run is the only execution path.
- Add tests proving graph selection does not alter chat query scope.
- Add tests proving text-derived tags appear in confirmation card scope when present.
- Add tests proving compliance requests without a loaded standard pack return missing capability.
- Add demo standard pack tests proving the demo pump discharge check can run and returns evidence.
- Add graph modernization tests at semantic UI seams: graph panel hidden initially, opens after upload, can be manually toggled, auto-opens for evidence, and renders typed node shapes/labels.
- Avoid brittle visual pixel tests for graph layout. Assert semantic node class-to-shape mapping, labels, visibility, toggle state, and evidence highlight classes.

## Out of Scope

- Open general-purpose chatbot behavior.
- Legal or production EPA compliance claims.
- Full authoritative EPA 60 implementation.
- User-uploaded arbitrary standard text becoming trusted compliance logic.
- Layout-faithful reconstruction of the original P&ID drawing.
- PDF, image, SVG, or multimodal diagram extraction.
- Direct graph-click-to-query scope in OSS v1.
- Mandatory Improve button in the first confirmation-card implementation.
- Large Python compiler from all possible structured intents to Datalog.
- Proving generated Datalog semantic correctness automatically.
- Model-controlled tool execution without backend validation and user approval.
- Replacing the existing Python backend workflow with MCP/session-registry/subprocess harness architecture.

## Further Notes

The agreed trust model is: LLM owns query drafting, user owns semantic approval, Python owns execution safety and result contract. This intentionally trusts the model for semantic drafting when it has the predicate and EDB context, while still preventing silent arbitrary execution.

The graph work should not be allowed to block the confirmation workflow. The immediate product issue is that users need to see and approve generated Datalog before execution. Graph modernization can follow as a separate slice using GraphML/Cytoscape and process-engineer visual language.

The accepted web review shell ADR remains in force: the primary product is a repository-owned Python backend plus React/TypeScript frontend. Chainlit remains a prototype shell only.
