title: PRD: Witness-grounded conversational P&ID QA
description:
## Problem Statement

Process engineers need to ask open-ended questions about an uploaded DEXPI source and receive useful natural-language answers without learning NetworkX, Datalog, or a domain-specific query language. The current workflow can prepare one source, generate and confirm Datalog, execute it, and return evidence, but it treats generated logic as the center of the backend. It does not yet provide a web-native model harness that can plan read-only topology retrieval, maintain conversational follow-ups, distinguish explicit from inferred engineering conclusions, or connect each answer claim to a complete structural witness.

The pyDEXPI full graph mirrors the source model and contains structural chains through nozzles, piping connections, piping nodes, network segments, equipment, and instrumentation. Simplifying those chains into a second engineering graph would hide information needed to justify topology answers and rule outcomes. A process-facing conclusion must therefore remain an interpretation of the pyDEXPI full graph and retain its complete structural path witness.

The product must also acknowledge inherent model risk. The application can constrain tools, execution, evidence, provenance, permissions, and confirmation, but it cannot guarantee model intelligence or prescribe every conversational response. The product needs a clear boundary where the model owns language interpretation, bounded retrieval planning, ambiguity handling, and prose while the backend owns deterministic evidence and execution controls.

## Solution

Build a witness-grounded, web-native QA harness over the existing pyDEXPI full graph. The application exposes constrained read-only topology and bundled-rule tools to native tool-capable models. The model chooses which tools to call, may perform a bounded sequence of retrievals, handles ambiguity conversationally, and writes a natural-language answer from returned evidence. The backend validates every tool call, applies resource and evidence budgets, preserves provenance, and streams typed conversation, turn, item, review, and completion events to the React frontend.

Keep the pyDEXPI full NetworkX graph as the only graph representation. Introduce a shared topology interpretation layer that computes process-facing relationships from raw paths and returns every conclusion with its complete ordered structural witness. Classify direction as explicit, inferred, or unknown. When inferred direction is necessary, let the user inspect the highlighted path and confirm, reverse, or mark the direction unknown through a session-scoped review annotation that never mutates source evidence.

Allow read-only retrieval and trusted repository-bundled rule execution to run immediately. Expose generated Datalog as a confirmation-required model capability used when read-only tools are insufficient. The generated query and engineer-readable restatement form one exact temporary query pair. Backend safety validation and explicit user confirmation are required before execution. Generated logic is never promoted into a reusable rule in OSS v1.

Return rule evaluations as justified satisfied, violated, or indeterminate outcomes. Every outcome includes evidence. Absence-based violations require a complete bounded evaluation scope and evidence explaining why traversal was complete. Apply claim-aware truncation so all grounded partial evidence is reported, while partial coverage never establishes a universal or absence conclusion.

Present answers as natural language with claim-level evidence chips. Selecting a chip opens the topology view, highlights the structural witness, and exposes evidence details. The model may provide useful chip labels, while backend metadata remains authoritative for provenance, direction, review status, and limitations.

OSS v1 permits one successfully prepared DEXPI XML source file per chat, not one guaranteed drawing page. Preparation is protected by configurable input, XML, graph, artifact, and execution resource limits. Pairwise comparison, multi-source projects, bulk checking, user-uploaded executable rule packs, policy-document ingestion, and reusable-rule authoring remain future workflows.

## User Stories

1. As a process engineer, I want to ask questions in ordinary language, so that I do not need to learn NetworkX or Datalog syntax.
2. As a process engineer, I want the model to choose appropriate read-only topology tools, so that the conversation remains flexible.
3. As a process engineer, I want direct topology questions answered without Datalog confirmation, so that simple questions remain fast.
4. As a process engineer, I want explanatory questions answered from bounded topology evidence, so that explanations remain grounded.
5. As a process engineer, I want formal or recursive questions to escalate to generated Datalog when necessary, so that complex reasoning remains available.
6. As a process engineer, I want generated Datalog to require confirmation, so that model-proposed logic never executes silently.
7. As a process engineer, I want the generated query and engineer-readable restatement approved together, so that executable logic cannot drift from reviewed meaning.
8. As a process engineer, I want confirmation to mean execution consent for the current query, so that temporary questions are not mistaken for reusable rules.
9. As a process engineer, I want repository-bundled rules to execute immediately, so that trusted repeated checks do not require unnecessary confirmation.
10. As a process engineer, I want every process-facing relationship backed by its complete structural path, so that simplified conclusions remain auditable.
11. As a process engineer, I want nozzle, connection, segment, and piping-node evidence retained, so that required structural relationships are not hidden.
12. As a process engineer, I want explicit and inferred flow direction distinguished, so that assumptions are visible.
13. As a process engineer, I want unknown direction reported honestly, so that missing source information is not replaced with certainty.
14. As a process engineer, I want to inspect inferred direction in the graph, so that I can use engineering judgment.
15. As a process engineer, I want to confirm inferred direction, so that an otherwise indeterminate question can continue.
16. As a process engineer, I want to reverse an incorrect inferred direction, so that the answer uses my reviewed interpretation.
17. As a process engineer, I want to mark direction unknown, so that I am not forced into a false binary choice.
18. As a process engineer, I want reviewed direction stored only as a session annotation, so that source evidence remains unchanged.
19. As a process engineer, I want a direction annotation reused when the exact path and boundary are unchanged, so that I am not repeatedly asked the same question.
20. As a process engineer, I want changed paths or boundaries to invalidate prior direction review, so that stale judgments are not silently reused.
21. As a process engineer, I want ambiguous object references handled conversationally, so that the chat does not feel like a rigid form.
22. As a process engineer, I want answers for multiple plausible candidates when practical, so that ambiguity can still produce useful information.
23. As a process engineer, I want inferred object interpretation disclosed, so that I can correct the model naturally.
24. As a process engineer, I want follow-up questions to understand prior turns, so that I can say “what about the other pump?” or “why did you infer that?”
25. As a process engineer, I want prior evidence reusable by reference, so that follow-ups remain grounded without repeating the entire explanation.
26. As a process engineer, I want prior model prose treated only as conversation context, so that earlier unsupported wording never becomes engineering evidence.
27. As a process engineer, I want long conversations compacted without losing my decisions, so that follow-ups remain coherent.
28. As a process engineer, I want evidence identities, confirmations, annotations, and limitations preserved through compaction, so that provenance survives long chats.
29. As a process engineer, I want streamed responses and tool progress, so that the web chat remains responsive during multi-step work.
30. As a process engineer, I want paused review actions to survive refresh or reconnect, so that confirmation work is not lost.
31. As a process engineer, I want to cancel an active turn, so that I remain in control of long-running work.
32. As a process engineer, I want natural-language answers rather than raw JSON, so that results are readable.
33. As a process engineer, I want claim-level evidence chips, so that I can inspect why a specific statement was made.
34. As a process engineer, I want an evidence chip to open and highlight the supporting graph path, so that prose and topology remain connected.
35. As a process engineer, I want evidence chips to disclose inferred, explicit, user-confirmed, rule-scope, and limitation metadata, so that evidence types are not conflated.
36. As a process engineer, I want unfamiliar evidence types to remain inspectable, so that the answer does not fail because presentation metadata evolved.
37. As a process engineer, I want every rule outcome to be satisfied, violated, or indeterminate, so that “no finding” is not treated as proof.
38. As a process engineer, I want satisfied outcomes justified by matching evidence, so that passing results are auditable.
39. As a process engineer, I want absence-based violations justified by an exhaustively evaluated bounded scope, so that incomplete traversal is not called a violation.
40. As a process engineer, I want missing start, direction, termination, or completeness evidence to produce an indeterminate result, so that uncertainty remains explicit.
41. As a process engineer, I want all grounded partial evidence reported when limits are reached, so that useful work is not discarded.
42. As a process engineer, I want partial coverage prevented from proving universal or absence claims, so that truncation does not create false certainty.
43. As a process engineer, I want witnessed counterexamples to disprove universal claims when logically sufficient, so that valid negative evidence is still useful.
44. As a process engineer, I want general P&ID and process-engineering questions answered from model knowledge, so that the assistant remains educational.
45. As a process engineer, I want general-knowledge source posture disclosed, so that educational guidance is not confused with loaded-source evidence.
46. As a process engineer, I want source-specific calculations to disclose missing operating data, so that the model does not invent inputs.
47. As a process engineer, I want unrelated questions redirected toward P&ID work, so that the product remains focused without rigid topic forms.
48. As an OSS user, I want to select any native tool-capable model offered through my configured provider, so that I retain model choice.
49. As an OSS user, I want models without native tool calling disregarded, so that unsupported models do not enter a broken workflow.
50. As an OSS user, I do not want model quality scores or certification badges, so that the product does not imply guarantees it cannot make.
51. As an OSS user, I want runtime model capability failures shown clearly, so that provider or metadata drift is understandable.
52. As an OSS user, I want one DEXPI source file per chat, so that source and conversation scope remain clear.
53. As an OSS user, I want the system to accept a broad valid conceptual model without pretending it is one graphical page, so that DEXPI semantics are respected.
54. As an OSS user, I want oversized sources rejected with explicit resource diagnostics, so that preparation does not fail mysteriously.
55. As an OSS user, I want failed uploads retryable before a source is established, so that corrected input does not require restarting the app.
56. As an OSS user, I want bundled demo rule packs clearly labeled non-authoritative, so that examples are not mistaken for certified compliance logic.
57. As an OSS user, I want the pack mechanism to support multiple packs and rules, so that additional examples can be added without redesign.
58. As an OSS user, I want at least one complete pump discharge check-valve rule, so that the grounded rule workflow is demonstrable end to end.
59. As an OSS user, I do not want uploaded executable rule packs accepted in v1, so that ungoverned logic cannot become trusted.
60. As an OSS user, I do not want uploaded policy documents silently converted into rules, so that policy synthesis is not confused with trusted execution.
61. As a future CLI user, I want the CLI to consume the same backend run lifecycle, so that web and CLI answers use identical evidence boundaries.
62. As a developer, I want the pyDEXPI full graph to remain the only NetworkX graph, so that structural evidence is never lost through a second materialized graph.
63. As a developer, I want shared topology operations rather than consumer-specific traversal, so that NetworkX, Datalog, the model, and the frontend agree.
64. As a developer, I want source-qualified evidence identities, so that future multi-source projects do not require redesigning provenance.
65. As a developer, I want model planning separated from backend execution, so that conversational flexibility does not grant execution authority.
66. As a developer, I want application tools classified as allowed, confirmation-required, or denied, so that the model harness has an explicit permission boundary.
67. As a developer, I want arbitrary shell, filesystem, graph mutation, and unrestricted network tools unavailable, so that the harness remains domain-constrained.
68. As a developer, I want provider/model tool capability checked for the exact combination, so that provider-wide assumptions do not admit incompatible models.
69. As a developer, I want tool arguments and evidence references validated independently of model quality, so that application invariants remain deterministic.
70. As a developer, I want generated Datalog context limited to the predicate contract and relevant resolved identities, so that the full fact database is not sent by default.
71. As a developer, I want mechanical Datalog safety validation separated from semantic approval, so that backend guarantees remain honest.
72. As a developer, I want one server-owned conversation, turn, and item lifecycle, so that streaming, pause, resume, and future clients share a contract.
73. As a developer, I want idempotent resume and tool execution, so that reconnects do not duplicate work.
74. As a developer, I want resource and evidence budgets configurable, so that deployment limits can evolve without changing engineering semantics.
75. As a product owner, I want pairwise P&ID comparison treated as a separate future workflow, so that OSS v1 is not burdened with cross-source alignment.
76. As a product owner, I want bulk multi-source rule execution reserved for a future paid project workflow, so that OSS and paid capabilities have a meaningful boundary.
77. As a product owner, I want user rule-pack upload and policy-to-rule authoring reserved for a future paid tier, so that OSS v1 demonstrates rather than governs custom rules.

## Implementation Decisions

- Keep the accepted Python backend API plus React/TypeScript frontend architecture.
- Keep the pyDEXPI full NetworkX graph as the sole graph representation.
- Persist canonical base facts as the stable, provenance-preserving serialization of the pyDEXPI full graph.
- Build a shared topology interpretation layer over the pyDEXPI full graph rather than a materialized engineering graph.
- Return complete ordered structural path witnesses for every process-facing relationship.
- Treat process-facing relationships as computed conclusions, not independent source facts.
- Classify flow direction as explicit, inferred, or unknown.
- Keep direction evidence status separate from user review status.
- Store user-confirmed, reversed, or unknown direction as a session annotation attached to an exact path witness and evaluation boundary.
- Invalidate direction annotations on new source, changed path, or changed boundary.
- Expose application-owned read-only topology tools and let the model plan their bounded use.
- Do not build a deterministic intent compiler, topic classifier, or mandatory ambiguity-selection UI.
- Support bounded multi-candidate retrieval so the model can answer for several plausible objects.
- Require native tool calls and tool-result continuation. Do not parse text-only pseudo-tool calls.
- Filter model availability by exact provider/model tool capability metadata, following the Models.dev pattern.
- Treat runtime provider rejection as authoritative when capability metadata is stale.
- Do not expose model quality scores, tested badges, certification tiers, or hardcoded family blacklists.
- Keep grounding evaluations as internal regression tests rather than product eligibility gates.
- Implement a restricted grounded-QA harness with allowed, confirmation-required, and denied tools.
- Deny arbitrary shell, filesystem mutation, graph mutation, and unrestricted network tools.
- Apply configurable per-operation and per-turn budgets for steps, time, paths, rows, evidence objects, path length, and payload size.
- Apply claim-aware truncation based on logical claim type rather than response wording.
- Report all grounded evidence obtained, coverage, and explicit limitations.
- Expose generated Datalog as a confirmation-required model capability.
- Supply generated-query context with the predicate contract, output contract, execution restrictions, conversation context, and relevant identities already resolved through retrieval.
- Do not send the complete session fact database to the model by default.
- Validate generated Datalog mechanically for approved predicates, output shape, append-only behavior, syntax, filesystem and include restrictions, size, timeout, and row limits.
- Pair generated Datalog with an engineer-readable restatement and confirm the exact pair.
- Treat confirmation as temporary execution consent, not reusable-rule promotion.
- Allow trusted repository-bundled rule-pack rules to execute immediately.
- Support multiple bundled packs and rules while requiring one complete pump discharge check-valve rule initially.
- Represent every rule evaluation as satisfied, violated, or indeterminate with evidence.
- Require scope-completeness evidence for absence-based violations.
- Treat model-only direction inference as insufficient for a formal rule outcome until user-reviewed.
- Build a server-owned review-session, conversation, turn, item, approval, interruption, and completion lifecycle inspired by Codex App Server concepts without depending on its runtime.
- Stream server events to the web frontend; keep tool execution and agent state out of browser code.
- Use server-to-browser event streaming plus ordinary HTTP review actions initially.
- Persist paused run state and make resume, cancellation, and tool execution idempotent.
- Preserve prior turns for conversational follow-ups.
- Preserve user decisions, resolved objects, evidence identities, confirmations, annotations, and limitations as structured conversation state.
- Compact older prose when necessary without promoting model prose into evidence.
- Accept free-form model answer text with references to known evidence IDs.
- Validate evidence references without prescribing prose.
- Render natural-language answers with claim-level evidence chips rather than raw response envelopes.
- Let the model supply useful chip labels while backend metadata controls provenance, direction, review status, trust, and limitations.
- Make evidence chips open the topology panel, highlight the exact structural witness, and display details.
- Allow general P&ID and process-engineering education from model knowledge with disclosed source posture.
- Require witnessed evidence for claims about the loaded source.
- Keep model-led domain redirection conversational rather than deterministic.
- Limit OSS v1 to one successfully prepared DEXPI XML source file per chat.
- Do not equate one source file with one graphical Drawing element or page.
- Enforce configurable input bytes, XML complexity, parse and extraction time, graph size, artifact size, and preparation limits before or during source preparation.
- Keep source IDs in evidence and tool contracts to preserve a future path to multi-source projects.
- Treat pairwise comparison, multi-source projects, bulk checking, uploaded packs, policy ingestion, and rule authoring as separate future workflows.

## Testing Decisions

- Test externally visible behavior rather than private helper structure.
- Prefer browser-level tests for complete user workflows and backend integration tests for deterministic contracts.
- Reuse the existing Playwright review-workflow harness for upload, chat, confirmation, Run, evidence expansion, and graph interaction.
- Add browser tests for streamed model text, tool progress, conversational follow-ups, review pause/resume, cancellation, reconnect, and claim-level evidence chips.
- Add browser tests proving an evidence chip opens the topology panel, highlights the witness, and displays explicit or inferred metadata.
- Add browser tests for direction review choices and rerunning the original operation after review.
- Add backend API tests for conversation, turn, item, event, interruption, pause, resume, and idempotency contracts.
- Add integration tests for native tool-call handling through provider adapters rather than parsing model text.
- Add provider tests proving non-tool-capable model combinations are excluded and runtime capability rejection is normalized.
- Add topology-operation tests over accepted DEXPI fixtures for complete structural witnesses, direction status, multi-candidate retrieval, boundaries, branches, and cycles.
- Add annotation tests proving exact-witness reuse and invalidation on changed source, path, or boundary.
- Add rule tests covering satisfied, violated, and indeterminate outcomes for the same rule family.
- Add negative-rule tests proving absence-based violation requires scope-completeness evidence.
- Add claim-aware truncation tests for existential matches, universal counterexamples, incomplete universal coverage, incomplete absence coverage, and explanatory partial results.
- Add Datalog proposal tests proving the capability pauses for validation and confirmation rather than executing directly.
- Extend existing generated-Datalog safety tests for predicate vocabulary, output contract, syntax, append-only behavior, filesystem restrictions, timeout, and row limits.
- Add answer-synthesis tests proving only known evidence references are accepted and unknown evidence kinds degrade to generic presentation.
- Add conversational tests proving prior prose is not accepted as evidence while valid prior evidence IDs remain usable.
- Add compaction tests proving user decisions, evidence IDs, annotations, confirmations, and limitations survive.
- Add source-preparation tests for upload bytes, XML complexity, parse timeout, graph size, artifact size, and preparation timeout diagnostics.
- Keep the existing full-page DEXPI acceptance corpus as the primary realistic regression surface.
- Add synthetic boundary fixtures only where the accepted corpus cannot produce a required limit, ambiguity, branch, cycle, or indeterminate state.
- Keep model-behavior evals for unsupported source-specific calculations, invented plant facts, ambiguity, evidence use, and limitation disclosure as regression signals rather than product certification.
- Validate documentation terminology against the witness-grounded QA contract and accepted ADRs.

## Out of Scope

- A second materialized engineering or process graph.
- Treating graphical Drawing count as a reliable P&ID page or workload boundary.
- More than one uploaded DEXPI source per OSS v1 chat.
- Pairwise P&ID comparison in the initial workflow.
- Multi-source review projects and cross-source entity alignment.
- Bulk rule-pack execution across a source collection.
- User-uploaded executable rule packs.
- Policy or standards document ingestion.
- Automatic policy-to-rule synthesis.
- Generated-query promotion into reusable rules.
- Durable personal or organizational rule approval.
- Named-standard, EPA, legal, or regulatory certification claims for demo rules.
- Automatic graph mutation, P&ID editing, or correction.
- Hydraulic simulation or source-specific calculations without required data and tools.
- Text-only model fallback through pseudo-tool parsing.
- Model quality certification, ranking, scoring, or guaranteed correctness.
- A deterministic application-owned intent compiler or topic classifier.
- Mandatory structured candidate-selection controls for conversational ambiguity.
- Full fact-database disclosure to the model by default.
- Arbitrary shell, filesystem, graph mutation, or unrestricted network tools.
- A multi-agent reviewer hierarchy in OSS v1.
- Direct dependency on OpenCode or Codex agent runtimes.
- A layout-faithful reconstruction of the source P&ID drawing.

## Further Notes

The governing principle is to control what the application can control: source validation, tool permissions, execution, provenance, evidence, limits, confirmation, and presentation of uncertainty. Model interpretation and prose remain inherently probabilistic. The application must not hide model failures, but it also must not attempt to replace model intelligence with brittle deterministic routing.

The core grounding invariant is: a process-facing relationship without its complete structural path witness is not grounded.

The core rule invariant is: no violation found is not proof of satisfaction.

The core truncation invariant is: report all grounded evidence obtained, but never turn partial coverage into a universal or absence conclusion.

The web-native harness borrows lifecycle concepts from Codex App Server and permission concepts from OpenCode, while remaining a provider-neutral, domain-specific Python implementation.

Mike OSS and Harvey demonstrate that project-scoped multi-document chat can be effective, but P&ID comparison additionally requires separate graph namespaces, source-qualified evidence, and entity alignment. Future multi-source projects should contain independent source sessions rather than one merged graph.

description:

title: PRD: Add LLM-assisted logic requests for deterministic P&ID QA
description:
## Problem Statement

Process engineers and EPC users need a way to ask natural-language questions about P&IDs and turn informal review rules into executable deterministic checks without hand-writing Datalog. The current system already has a trusted DEXPI 1.3 source-file to graph-facts to derived Souffle predicate pipeline, plus deterministic query artifacts, but it requires humans to know the query corpus, predicate vocabulary, and Datalog-oriented execution seams.

The user wants frontier LLM assistance without making the LLM the compliance answer source. The LLM should help refine vague requests, route non-logic questions, draft Datalog for topology QA, and explain deterministic results. The answer source must remain deterministic execution over the approved predicate contract. Small customers should eventually use app-managed credits plus overage, while the first CLI slice can use OPENAI_API_KEY.

## Solution

Add a CLI-artifact logic workflow for LLM-assisted logic requests. A logic request starts as a user-authored natural-language request and may be refined, routed, drafted into generated Datalog plus an engineer-readable formal restatement, confirmed by the user, and then executed against an existing derived_graph_semantics.dl artifact.

The first implementation should be text-only, OpenAI-backed, and orchestrated by repository-owned Python code rather than autonomous agent tool use. The LLM may draft Datalog and restatements, but Python controls routing, validation, repair attempts, confirmation boundaries, Souffle execution, artifacts, and diagnostics. The deterministic result artifact remains primary; any final LLM explanation is supplemental.

V1 should support hybrid QA request routing. Not every request should become Datalog. Documentation and metadata questions can be answered through cheaper faithful paths. Unsupported engineering requests should produce missing-capability artifacts instead of invented answers. Topology QA logic requests should use only the approved predicate contract by default, with generic raw attributes gated behind an explicit advanced raw-attribute mode.

## User Stories

1. As a process engineer, I want to enter a natural-language P&ID question, so that I do not need to write Datalog by hand.
2. As a process engineer, I want vague requests to be refined before logic generation, so that the system does not guess hidden assumptions.
3. As a process engineer, I want the system to classify whether my request needs Datalog, metadata lookup, documentation, clarification, or is unsupported, so that not every question is forced into logic.
4. As a process engineer, I want the LLM to draft Datalog from a topology QA logic request, so that natural language can become executable deterministic logic.
5. As a process engineer, I want to review a formal restatement of the generated logic, so that I can confirm intent without reading Datalog.
6. As a process engineer, I want the formal restatement to include if-then conditions, negation, logical operators, exceptions, and scope, so that the rule semantics are inspectable.
7. As a process engineer, I want the system to execute generated Datalog only after I confirm the paired Datalog and restatement, so that logic does not run against my plant unexpectedly.
8. As a process engineer, I want deterministic query results to be shown before any LLM explanation, so that I can distinguish facts from prose.
9. As a process engineer, I want the LLM to explain deterministic results in plain language, so that I can understand the output without losing traceability.
10. As a process engineer, I want unsupported requests to return missing facts, missing predicates, missing policy, or external-tool requirements, so that I know what capability is absent.
11. As a process engineer, I want topology questions to run over approved graph and topology predicates, so that answers are grounded in the derived semantics layer.
12. As a process engineer, I want generic raw attribute querying to be opt-in, so that normal queries do not depend accidentally on messy source attribute names.
13. As a process engineer, I want the command to work against an existing derived_graph_semantics.dl file, so that I can use the artifact seam the repo already trusts.
14. As a process engineer, I want syntax and safety diagnostics before confirmation, so that I do not review invalid logic.
15. As a process engineer, I want generated Datalog repair attempts to be bounded, so that the system does not loop indefinitely or burn cost.
16. As a process engineer, I want documentation questions to be answered from project docs or predicate documentation, so that simple conceptual questions do not require Datalog execution.
17. As a process engineer, I want metadata questions to be answered from artifacts, so that I can inspect runs without invoking unnecessary logic generation.
18. As a process engineer, I want final artifacts to record which model and context policy were used, so that I can assess trust and reproducibility.
19. As a small-firm user, I want future product pricing to use app-managed credits plus overage, so that I do not have to manage provider API keys in the product.
20. As a CLI pilot user, I want to use OPENAI_API_KEY, so that early experiments can run before product billing exists.
21. As a tenant admin, I want full-topology model context to require explicit opt-in, so that sensitive plant topology is not sent to a provider by default.
22. As a tenant admin, I want a maximum LLM context policy, so that I can control whether the model receives only the predicate contract, scoped context, or full topology.
23. As a security reviewer, I want no full prompt transcript retained by default, so that prompt logs do not become a sensitive data archive.
24. As a security reviewer, I want a minimal logic-request audit record, so that routing, model, context policy, confirmation, artifacts, and diagnostics are traceable.
25. As a maintainer, I want the LLM provider behind an adapter, so that OpenAI can be replaced later by Azure OpenAI, Bedrock, Anthropic, or enterprise endpoints.
26. As a maintainer, I want v1 to avoid autonomous agent tool-calling, so that repository-owned code controls execution and artifacts.
27. As a maintainer, I want live OpenAI calls excluded from CI, so that tests are deterministic and do not require secrets.
28. As a maintainer, I want fake-provider tests, so that routing, drafting, repair, confirmation, and execution behavior can be validated without network calls.
29. As a maintainer, I want generated Datalog constrained to a safe Souffle subset, so that user-facing LLM-authored logic cannot include arbitrary includes, inputs, files, or external functors.
30. As a maintainer, I want generated helper predicates to be namespaced, so that LLM-authored relations do not collide with approved predicates.
31. As a maintainer, I want generated recursive predicates allowed with runtime limits, so that topology questions remain expressible.
32. As a maintainer, I want max output rows, Datalog size, relation count, and execution timeout limits, so that generated logic cannot create unbounded output or runaway execution.
33. As a future product owner, I want saved logic requests and standard rule packs deferred, so that v1 focuses on confirmed execution before persistence and promotion.
34. As a future product owner, I want the design to leave room for HAZOP and EPA-related standard rule packs, so that validated bundled checks can come later.
35. As a future enterprise buyer, I want deployment-tiered LLM privacy, so that small users can use managed APIs while larger firms can later use approved Azure, Bedrock, BYOC, VPC, or on-prem options.
36. As a future integration user, I want BioWin and simulation integrations deferred, so that v1 does not overclaim hydraulic or thermodynamic reasoning.
37. As a future multimodal user, I want image/SVG reasoning deferred, so that the initial trust boundary remains DEXPI XML to pyDEXPI graph to facts to Datalog.
38. As a reviewer, I want generated logic artifacts to be compact, so that the system does not produce excessive side files for every request.
39. As a reviewer, I want missing-capability artifacts to feed roadmap learning, so that unsupported questions reveal the next predicates or extraction projections needed.
40. As a reviewer, I want deterministic result artifacts and generated Datalog preserved, so that an answer can be reproduced and inspected later.

## Implementation Decisions

- The canonical product object is a logic request, not separate query and rule authoring flows.
- Saving logic requests for reuse is out of the first implementation; the user may eventually decide to save a confirmed logic request later.
- V1 is CLI-artifact-first rather than API/server-first.
- V1 adds an optional refine step that improves a vague logic request into a clearer request with assumptions, clarifying questions, route hints, and recommended scope.
- V1 adds a draft step that routes a logic request and, for topology logic, asks OpenAI to generate Datalog plus a formal engineer-readable restatement.
- V1 adds an execute step that requires confirmation before running generated Datalog against real derived graph semantics.
- The execution input is an existing derived_graph_semantics.dl artifact, not raw DEXPI XML.
- Python orchestrates the workflow. The LLM does not directly call Souffle, shell, filesystem, DEXPI extraction, BioWin, web search, or other tools.
- OpenAI is the first provider. The first CLI slice reads credentials from OPENAI_API_KEY.
- The model is configurable, with a high-accuracy default and cost optimization deferred.
- The provider integration should sit behind a small internal adapter. Do not adopt an agent framework for v1.
- V1 is text-only. Multimodal diagram, SVG, screenshot, and vision inputs are deferred.
- The router supports topology logic, metadata lookup, documentation answer, missing capability, clarification, and future external-tool-required outcomes.
- Only generated-Datalog requests require paired restatement confirmation.
- The LLM receives the predicate contract and synthetic tutorial facts by default, not customer plant facts.
- Tenant-level context policy should support contract-only, scoped-context, and full-topology levels. Full-topology context requires tenant admin opt-in in product form.
- No full prompt transcript is retained by default. Persist a minimal logic-request audit record instead.
- The draft artifact should be compact: one logic_request.json plus generated_query.dl as the only draft sidecar when needed.
- The formal restatement is stored inside the draft artifact rather than as many separate files in v1.
- The deterministic execution result remains primary. Any LLM explanation is supplemental.
- Generated Datalog uses only the approved predicate contract by default.
- Approved default predicates include node/1, node_label/2, node_tag/2, node_proteus_id/2, composition_edge/3, reference_edge/3, candidate_topology_edge/3, downstream_candidate/2, downstream_composition/2, downstream_reference/2, reachable/2, and direct_process_connection/2 marked experimental.
- Generic node_attribute/3 and graph_edge_attribute-style raw attributes are excluded by default and allowed only in advanced raw-attribute mode.
- Generated Datalog may define new namespaced helper predicates, including recursive helpers, if they compile and stay within runtime limits.
- Generated Datalog must not use .input, .include, external functors, arbitrary file paths, undeclared outputs, or relation names that collide with approved predicates.
- Safety checks enforce approved predicates, namespaced generated relations, declared output relations, maximum Datalog size, maximum generated relation count, timeout, and row limits.
- Repair attempts are bounded to two retries after an invalid generated program.
- Unsupported logic requests produce missing-capability artifacts rather than best-effort answers.
- Saved logic, trusted rule promotion, standard HAZOP/EPA rule packs, app-managed credits, BYOC, Azure OpenAI, AWS Bedrock, VPC deployment, and on-prem model deployment are future product work.

## Testing Decisions

- Tests should use the highest public seam: CLI commands and persisted artifacts.
- Tests should not assert private prompt construction details unless those details are part of a public artifact contract.
- Normal CI must not require a live OpenAI key or network access.
- Use a fake LLM provider for deterministic tests of routing, drafting, repair, restatement, confirmation, and execution behavior.
- Add a test seam for a mocked valid topology logic request that drafts Datalog and restatement into a compact logic request artifact.
- Add a test seam for an invalid generated Datalog response that enters a bounded repair loop and then succeeds or fails with diagnostics.
- Add a test seam for unknown predicate use that returns a missing-capability or safety diagnostic instead of executing.
- Add a test seam proving execute requires confirmation before running generated Datalog against derived semantics.
- Add a test seam proving confirmed generated Datalog runs against the checked-in derived graph semantics fixture and persists deterministic result artifacts.
- Add a test seam proving documentation and metadata requests route away from Datalog generation.
- Add a test seam proving raw attributes are rejected by default and allowed only in advanced raw-attribute mode.
- Add a test seam proving runtime guardrails such as output row limits, timeout configuration, and disallowed constructs are enforced at the command boundary.
- Existing prior art includes CLI and persisted-artifact tests for query-derived-graph, derive-graph-semantics, compile-rule, verify-suite, verify-raw-fixture, and review-only.
- Existing deterministic query artifacts provide a model for combined query Datalog, result JSON, diagnostics, and raw Souffle output directories.
- Live OpenAI quality should be evaluated through an optional manual eval command or fixture set, not required in CI.

## Out of Scope

- App/server UI.
- Product billing implementation.
- App-managed credit ledger.
- Customer API-key upload UI.
- Azure OpenAI, AWS Bedrock, BYOC, VPC, or on-prem deployment implementation.
- Anthropic provider support in v1.
- Agent frameworks such as LangChain, LlamaIndex, OpenAI Agents SDK, Cline as runtime dependency, or autonomous tool-calling agents.
- Multimodal P&ID image/SVG/screenshot reasoning.
- Raw DEXPI XML execution input for logic requests.
- One-command raw DEXPI to LLM logic execution workflow.
- BioWin or other process simulation integrations.
- Hydraulic, thermodynamic, sizing, or EPA/HAZOP compliance packs.
- Standard rule-pack authoring and promotion lifecycle.
- Saving logic requests for reuse.
- Deterministic Datalog-to-English compiler.
- Full prompt transcript retention by default.
- Full-topology prompt context by default.
- LLM-generated patch proposals or autocorrection.

## Further Notes

The central product principle remains unchanged: deterministic execution answers compliance and engineering logic questions; the LLM may refine, route, draft, repair, restate, and explain, but it is not the answer source.

The first implementation should optimize for learning whether frontier models can reliably draft useful Datalog against the repo-owned predicate contract. The CLI-artifact workflow should preserve enough evidence to debug failures without turning prompt logs into sensitive archives.

The long-term product can evolve toward app-managed credits plus overage for small customers, enterprise model/provider controls for larger customers, standard rule packs for recognized review frameworks, and private deployment options. Those future tiers should reuse the same logic-request, predicate-contract, confirmation, and deterministic execution concepts proven by the CLI slice.

title: PRD: Establish the DEXPI 1.3 graph-mirrored fact substrate and derived Souffle semantics
description:
## Problem Statement

Process engineering teams need a deterministic substrate for logical
programming over DEXPI 1.3 P&IDs before they can trust richer operator-facing
verification workflows.

The current repository already has useful scaffolding, a graph-mirrored export
seed, and an initial tracer-bullet verifier. What it does not yet have is a
fully explicit contract for turning the supported DEXPI 1.3 fixture corpus into
graph-mirrored facts and then deriving reusable Souffle semantics from those
facts. Without that substrate, later rule work risks drifting into ad hoc
predicate design, fixture-specific shortcuts, or AI-generated rules without a
stable deterministic execution boundary.

## Solution

Build the next verifier substrate slice around DEXPI 1.3 graph-mirrored facts
and derived Souffle graph semantics.

The solution should treat `pyDEXPI` as the trusted extraction dependency for
DEXPI 1.3 XML-to-graph conversion, persist a verbose and generic canonical base
fact layer over the `pyDEXPI` full graph, and add a hand-authored generic graph
utility layer plus repo-owned edge-family classification policy in Souffle.

This slice should prove the substrate over the parseable DEXPI 1.3 fixture
corpus, document the contract sharply, and establish the behavioral test seams
that later pump-specific rules, rule packs, and AI-assisted rule synthesis can
rely on.

## User Stories

1. As a process engineer, I want DEXPI 1.3 to be the explicit authoritative input contract, so that the repository does not imply support for a different semantic ingestion model than the code actually uses.
2. As a maintainer, I want `pyDEXPI` to be treated as the trusted DEXPI 1.3 XML-to-graph extraction dependency, so that the project boundary between extraction and interpretation stays explicit.
3. As a rules author, I want the canonical base fact layer to mirror the `pyDEXPI` full graph, so that every downstream rule begins from a reproducible graph substrate.
4. As a rules author, I want the base export to remain intentionally verbose and generic, so that I do not lose evidence through premature schema curation.
5. As a maintainer, I want one persisted fact per extracted node, one per extracted edge, and one per attached attribute, so that the fact grain remains stable and auditable.
6. As a maintainer, I want previously unseen upstream attributes to survive export automatically, so that new DEXPI 1.3 fixture shapes do not break the substrate.
7. As a rules author, I want the base export to avoid convenience predicates such as `pump/1`, so that interpretation stays out of the persisted contract.
8. As a maintainer, I want the contract to be defined over the parseable DEXPI 1.3 fixture corpus, so that the substrate proves itself against real fixture breadth rather than one narrow example.
9. As a reviewer, I want the checked-in golden fixtures to be clearly documented as a seed set rather than the full contract boundary, so that future work does not mistake current goldens for full coverage.
10. As a rules author, I want the first derived Souffle layer to be generic and reusable, so that later rule families can build on it without rewriting graph logic.
11. As a rules author, I want reusable edge-family predicates such as `composition_edge/3` and `reference_edge/3`, so that downstream rules do not repeatedly join raw edge attributes by hand.
12. As a rules author, I want a cautious `candidate_topology_edge/3` predicate, so that topology traversal can begin before the project commits to a stronger process-topology interpretation.
13. As a rules author, I want family-specific direct adjacency helpers, so that each rule can choose the correct traversal semantics explicitly.
14. As a rules author, I want a simple recursive `reachable/2` predicate over candidate topology edges, so that I can ask whether something is downstream without building full path provenance first.
15. As a maintainer, I want the first utility layer to stay small and explicit, so that it does not accumulate broad helper predicates before real rules require them.
16. As a maintainer, I want the edge-family classification policy to live in Souffle, so that interpretation can evolve without changing the persisted export format.
17. As a reviewer, I want the derived graph semantics contract to name the initial predicate surface explicitly, so that the next implementation slice cannot drift into vague “some utilities later” language.
18. As a process engineer, I want verification to be documented as downstream of graph export plus derived semantics, so that the architecture is understood as layered rather than verifier-first.
19. As a maintainer, I want the contract docs to state clearly that convenience predicates and domain predicates belong in derived Souffle layers, so that no one silently moves interpretation into the exporter.
20. As a maintainer, I want outdated `DEXPI 2.0 semantic IR` language removed from the active glossary and contract docs, so that the written architecture matches the implemented boundary.
21. As a rules author, I want the first validation seam to be stable graph export over the DEXPI 1.3 corpus, so that later logic failures can be isolated from extraction/export failures.
22. As a rules author, I want the second validation seam to be focused tests over representative fixtures such as `E03`, `E06`, and `C01`, so that recursive and classified predicates can be checked against real graph shapes.
23. As a maintainer, I want synthetic examples to remain available for later isolated rule verification, so that future rule generation can be tested behaviorally and not only on noisy corpus fixtures.
24. As a future operator, I want later trusted rules to execute deterministically over the fact layer instead of relying on ad hoc AI answers, so that verification remains reproducible and auditable.
25. As a future AI-assisted rules author, I want a stable graph-mirrored substrate and reusable graph utilities, so that generated rules have a deterministic target surface to compile against.
26. As a compliance engineer, I want rule packs to remain distinct from policy source documents, so that natural-language standards can later synthesize candidate rules without being confused for executable logic.
27. As a reviewer, I want AI-generated rules to be treated as candidates that require behavioral examples, so that trust comes from deterministic execution rather than raw Datalog readability.
28. As a maintainer, I want the next slice to defer policy-document-to-rule-pack synthesis, so that the foundational substrate work is not swallowed by a much larger AI problem.
29. As a maintainer, I want the repo PRD and Beads issue record to describe the same substrate plan, so that future contributors do not read contradictory planning artifacts.
30. As an engineer extending the verifier later, I want explicit derived graph semantics contracts in the docs, so that new rule families can reuse the same vocabulary and testing seams.

## Implementation Decisions

- The authoritative input contract for this slice is DEXPI 1.3 only.
- `pyDEXPI` is the trusted extraction dependency for XML-to-graph conversion; this repository owns graph-to-facts export and Souffle-derived interpretation above that export.
- The canonical persisted layer is a graph-mirrored base fact layer over the `pyDEXPI` full graph rather than a raw XML fact tree or an early domain-curated schema.
- The canonical base fact layer is intentionally verbose and generic. It should preserve extracted nodes, extracted edges, and attached attributes without introducing rule-specific predicates.
- Unknown or newly observed upstream attributes should survive export automatically through generic attribute facts rather than causing schema failures.
- The canonical base layer should persist only the `pyDEXPI` full graph for now. Explicit raw XML containment facts are deferred unless a concrete future rule proves they are needed.
- The intended regression surface for the substrate is the parseable DEXPI 1.3 fixture corpus, not only the current `E03`, `E06`, and `C01` golden seed set.
- The first derived Souffle layer should be hand-authored rather than generated from observed graph schema.
- The repo-owned classification policy should live in Souffle rather than in exporter code, so classified semantics can evolve without re-exporting the canonical fact layer.
- The initial derived predicate surface should be explicit: `composition_edge/3`, `reference_edge/3`, `candidate_topology_edge/3`, `downstream_candidate/2`, `downstream_composition/2`, `downstream_reference/2`, and `reachable/2`.
- `candidate_topology_edge/3` should be intentionally conservative rather than claiming that topology traversal is already fully trusted in every case.
- Direct adjacency helpers should stay family-specific. Broader union predicates such as `downstream/2` should be introduced only when a real rule or operator-facing query needs them.
- The first recursive utility should be `reachable/2` over `candidate_topology_edge/3`; ordered path reconstruction and full path provenance are deferred.
- Pump discharge YAML rules should sit above the generic base fact layer and derived graph semantics layer rather than embedding graph semantics themselves.
- Verification commands should be documented and treated as consumers of the export-plus-derived-semantics substrate, not as the primary architectural center.
- The rule trust model for later AI-assisted work should be behavioral: candidate rules become trustworthy only after deterministic execution against positive and negative examples.
- Single rules and rule packs remain distinct units. Individual rules are the unit of behavioral debugging; rule packs are the unit of versioned promotion and deployment.
- Policy source documents, rule packs, and rule-pack synthesis are distinct concepts and should remain separate in the glossary and contract docs.

## Testing Decisions

- Good tests should assert external behavior and stable contracts, not implementation details or private helper structure.
- The highest seam for this slice is the `export-facts` behavior over the parseable DEXPI 1.3 fixture corpus. Tests at this seam should verify deterministic persisted graph-mirrored facts, provenance, and automatic preservation of observed attributes.
- A second high seam should cover the derived graph semantics layer on representative fixtures such as `E03`, `E06`, and `C01`, validating classified edge families, family-specific downstream helpers, and recursive `reachable/2`.
- Later synthetic examples should be used for isolated rule-shape verification, but the current substrate slice should prefer real DEXPI 1.3 fixtures wherever possible.
- Tests should confirm that the base export does not emit convenience predicates or domain predicates in the persisted artifact contract.
- Tests should verify that the current checked-in golden fixtures remain a seed set and that broader corpus coverage can be expanded without redefining the base contract.
- Tests should confirm that the derived classification policy lives above the persisted export and can change without changing the base fact artifact shape.
- Documentation-facing tests or fixture assertions should continue to use the repo’s existing black-box style around CLI commands and persisted artifacts rather than internal function mocks.
- Prior art already exists in the repository for export-facts CLI tests, checked-in golden graph facts, compile-rule CLI tests, and verifier-suite artifact tests. The new tests should extend those existing seams instead of inventing lower-level unit seams.
- Future AI-assisted rule verification should rely on positive and negative examples evaluated by the deterministic engine, not human review of raw Datalog syntax.

## Out of Scope

- DEXPI 2.0 as an active ingestion contract.
- A raw XML fact layer or XML-tree-first substrate.
- Automatic generation of domain predicates from unseen graph shapes.
- Full path reconstruction or ordered path evidence in the first derived utility slice.
- Pump-specific or rule-specific domain predicates in the persisted base export.
- DEXPI 1.2 as part of the current canonical substrate contract.
- Policy-document-to-rule-pack synthesis.
- Operator-facing dropdown UX for rule or rule-pack selection.
- Trusting AI to answer operator verification questions directly without deterministic execution.
- Human approval workflows for AI-generated rules beyond the defined behavioral-verification model.

## Further Notes

- The most important architectural protection in this slice is the boundary between generic persisted facts and derived Souffle interpretation.
- The base fact layer should be allowed to be verbose if that preserves reproducibility and future extensibility.
- The current checked-in documentation cleanup is part of the work because stale contract language would otherwise undermine the implementation slice.
- This PRD intentionally narrows the next step to substrate work. Richer operator rules, compliance rule packs, and AI-assisted synthesis remain downstream consumers of this layer rather than part of it.
